screens.title: Database Migration Service and Schema Conversion Tool
screens.narratorSegment: Migrating a running database to AWS is one of the most concrete problems a solutions architect will solve. In this lesson you'll see the complementary roles of AWS Database Migration Service and the Schema Conversion Tool. DMS is designed to move and synchronize data reliably across engines and platforms, while SCT focuses on converting schema elements and custom database code when engines differ. Together they reduce downtime by letting you perform a full initial copy and then continuously replicate changes until cutover. We'll highlight common migration types, the core components you must configure, and the practical trade-offs you will face, such as replication instance sizing, endpoint security, and validation. You will also be shown a short conceptual walkthrough that mirrors a real migration: prepare source and target, run schema conversion for heterogeneous moves, then use DMS to perform a full load followed by change data capture to keep systems in sync. By the end of this module you'll understand when to use SCT, how DMS handles continuous replication, and what testing and validation steps prevent common failures during cutover. Consider one immediate question as you begin: what level of downtime can your application tolerate?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify migration challenges, explain DMS capabilities, use SCT for heterogeneous conversions, and design a migration strategy that balances downtime and risk. First, you'll learn to identify common challenges like data integrity, compatibility between engines, and limiting downtime. Recognizing these problems helps you pick the right migration type and tools. Second, you'll learn how DMS supports both homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations, how it moves data, and how continuous replication keeps target systems synchronized. Third, you'll practice using the Schema Conversion Tool to assess and convert schema and custom code when engines differ. This helps you estimate manual work and prioritize tests. Fourth, you'll design a migration approach that combines a full initial load, Change Data Capture for ongoing changes, and data validation to confirm correctness. Each objective focuses on real decisions you must make: what to convert automatically, how to size a replication instance, and how to secure endpoints. These skills let you plan migrations that meet business downtime constraints while protecting application behavior and data integrity.

screens.title: Objectives — deep dive
screens.narratorSegment: Let's take those objectives a layer deeper and relate them to concrete tasks you'll perform. When you identify migration challenges you will inventory schema, stored code, and data volume, and then define acceptable downtime. That inventory informs whether you need SCT for code conversion. When you explain DMS capabilities you will choose between homogeneous moves where only data transfer is required, and heterogeneous moves where schema conversion is essential. Practically, that means using DMS replication instances to carry data, and configuring endpoints and tasks with appropriate table mappings. When using SCT, you'll run an assessment report that highlights items requiring manual conversion; you will use that report to estimate engineering effort and prioritize tests. Finally, when designing a migration strategy you'll size the replication instance, enable encryption and VPC connectivity for endpoints, and enable DMS validation to compare source and target rows. Each objective ties to a verification step: run test migrations, exercise the application against the target, and perform a final validation before cutover. These steps reduce surprises and protect production traffic during migration.

screens.title: Migration challenges and goals
screens.narratorSegment: Migrating a production database is not just a data copy exercise — it's an exercise in preserving application behavior, integrity, and availability. The core challenges are maintaining data integrity across millions of rows, minimizing downtime so user-facing systems remain responsive, and handling compatibility issues between database engines if you change platforms. For many organizations the highest priority is limiting the cutover window so the business isn't disrupted. That requirement drives the use of an initial full load followed by continuous replication. A concrete example is a web application backed by an on-premises Oracle database that must move to PostgreSQL on RDS. You cannot simply copy data; stored procedures and proprietary S Q L might behave differently on the target. This is where assessments and tools become critical: the Schema Conversion Tool analyzes schema and code, identifying items that can be converted automatically and those that will need manual work. A common misconception is thinking that data movement alone solves migration — in heterogeneous scenarios, schema and code conversion are equally important. The takeaway is to treat migration as a systems project: inventory, plan for compatibility, and design for validation and rollback before you run the first replication task.

keyIdea.text: Migration must preserve data, behavior, and availability; plan for compatibility and validation, not only transfer.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Migration challenges
Core definition

Database migration involves moving data and preserving application behavior while minimizing downtime and addressing compatibility between source and target engines.

Why it matters
  • Data integrity prevents corruption and business errors.
  • Minimal downtime keeps customer-facing services available.
  • Schema and code compatibility avoid runtime failures after cutover.
Common misconception

Assuming data copy alone is sufficient. In heterogeneous migrations you also must convert schema and custom code with SCT or manual effort.

Concrete example

Moving an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL requires schema conversion for PL/SQL and function logic; otherwise application behavior may change after cutover.

Key Takeaway

Treat migration as a system change: inventory, convert schema when needed, replicate data reliably, and validate before cutover.

screens.title: What is AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Database Migration Service is a managed service that performs the heavy lifting of moving data between sources and targets. At heart, DMS orchestrates a replication instance that connects to a source endpoint and a target endpoint, reads data from the source, and applies it to the target. It supports relational databases, data warehouses, NoSQL stores, and other data stores. A homogeneous migration is straightforward because the engines match — DMS focuses on data transfer, optionally with minor schema adjustments. For heterogeneous migrations DMS still moves the data, but schema and code conversion are handled by the Schema Conversion Tool. A practical sketch of the DMS architecture helps: replication instances are managed compute resources that run migration tasks, endpoints store connection details and credentials, and replication tasks define which tables to migrate and whether to capture ongoing changes. A common pitfall is under-sizing the replication instance. If the instance can't keep up, the migration is slow and CDC lag grows. The important takeaway is to treat DMS as an orchestration platform — configure instance size, secure endpoints inside your VPC, and enable validation to ensure the target matches the source.

keyIdea.title: What DMS does
keyIdea.text: DMS runs replication instances that move and synchronize data between source and target endpoints; configure tasks for full load, CDC, and validation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › DMS Overview
DMS definition

DMS is a managed migration service that uses replication instances to move and synchronize data between source and target endpoints, supporting full loads and continuous replication.

Components
  • Replication instance: the compute that performs migrations.
  • Endpoints: connection info for source and target databases.
  • Replication tasks: rules for what and how to migrate.
Pitfall

Choosing too small a replication instance creates bottlenecks and CDC lag. Size for expected throughput and peak load during cutover testing.

Concrete scenario

You have MySQL on EC2 and an RDS MySQL target. Create a replication instance, define source and target endpoints with credentials, and run a replication task to do full load then CDC to minimize downtime.

Key Takeaway

Treat DMS as both a data mover and an orchestrator; configure its components to match your migration throughput and security needs.

screens.title: Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous migrations
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding whether you're performing a homogeneous or heterogeneous migration is one of the first architectural decisions you must make. A homogeneous migration occurs when source and target engines are the same, for example MySQL to MySQL. In that case, your primary work is transferring data; DMS handles the copy, continuous replication, and validation with minimal schema conversion. A heterogeneous migration happens when database engines differ, such as Oracle to PostgreSQL or S Q L Server to MySQL. Heterogeneous moves are more complex because schema structures, data types, and procedural code differ. DMS remains responsible for data movement, but schema and code conversion requires the Schema Conversion Tool. SCT analyzes the source schema and custom database code, automatically converts compatible elements, and produces an assessment report that flags items needing manual attention. A concrete example: migrating Oracle PL/S Q L packages to PostgreSQL functions may require manual rewriting for complex logic; SCT will identify those functions and estimate conversion work. A common misconception is believing DMS will convert all stored code automatically — it will not. The practical consequence is to run SCT early, estimate manual effort, and reserve time for testing and application adjustments before cutover.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous
Homogeneous migration

Source and target engines are the same. DMS primarily moves data and can handle schema differences that are minor.

  • Example: MySQL on EC2 → RDS MySQL
  • Focus: replication instance sizing and endpoint security
Takeaway

Homogeneous moves are simpler and usually need less manual conversion work.

Heterogeneous migration

Source and target engines differ. Use SCT to convert schema and most custom code, then use DMS for data movement and CDC.

  • Example: Oracle → PostgreSQL
  • Focus: SCT assessment, manual conversion for flagged items, and thorough testing
Common mistake

Assuming SCT will convert every proprietary function. Use the SCT report to plan manual rewrites for complex logic.

screens.title: DMS components explained
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable migration requires understanding the three pillars of DMS: replication instance, endpoints, and replication tasks. The replication instance is managed compute that reads from the source and writes to the target. You choose an instance class based on throughput and latency requirements; under-sizing commonly causes replication lag. Endpoints capture connection details for source and target databases — host, port, credentials, and engine type — and they should be secured inside your VPC with proper security groups. Replication tasks bind these together and define what to move and how: table mappings, filters, transformation rules, and the migration type. DMS supports full load, change data capture, or full-load plus CDC. For a typical low-downtime strategy you run a full load to copy existing rows, then enable CDC to apply ongoing changes until the target is caught up. A practical check: enable data validation in the replication task to compare rows and catch drift. A misconception to avoid is treating replication tasks as a one-time setting; refine mappings and validation rules during testing to ensure the target schema receives data in the expected shape. The core insight is that correct configuration across these components prevents surprises during cutover.

keyIdea.text: Replication instance executes migration; endpoints store connection details; tasks define scope, type, and validation rules.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › DMS Components
Replication instance

Managed EC2-like compute that runs migration tasks. Size it for throughput to avoid CDC lag during heavy changes.

Endpoints

Connection definitions for source and target databases. Configure in-VPC connectivity and security groups to protect credentials and traffic.

Takeaway

Tune each component: instance class for performance, endpoints for security, and tasks for correctness and validation.

Replication tasks

Tasks define table mappings, filters, and migration type. Enable data validation to compare source and target rows and flag mismatches.

Concrete example

Create a replication task with table-mappings to migrate all tables in a schema, set migration-type to full-load-and-cdc, and enable validation in task settings.

Common mistake

Not enabling validation or not testing mappings results in silent schema drift and application errors after cutover.

screens.title: Migration types: Full load and Change Data Capture
screens.narratorSegment: A low-downtime migration commonly uses a two-phase approach: an initial full load followed by Change Data Capture. The full load copies existing rows from source to target; CDC then streams new and changed transactions to the target so it stays synchronized. In practice you start by creating endpoints, sizing your replication instance, and running a replication task in full-load-and-cdc mode. The full load runs first and populates the target. CDC continues to capture inserts, updates, and deletes on the source until you are ready to cut over. This approach lets you test the application on the target while production continues to write to the source. A concrete example: copy a million-row orders table during off-peak hours, then enable CDC to apply ongoing orders as they arrive. Once the target is fully caught up, perform a short maintenance window for final validation and switch application connectivity. A common misconception is relying on CDC alone to reconstruct historical state; CDC only captures changes from a start position and does not replace a full initial load for historical data. The key insight is to coordinate full load, CDC, and validation to achieve a predictable cutover with minimal downtime.

keyIdea.title: Migration type
keyIdea.text: Use full load to copy existing data, then CDC to capture ongoing changes until cutover — combined they minimize downtime.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Full load + CDC
Step-by-step
  1. Prepare source and target and ensure network connectivity.
  2. Create replication instance and endpoints with secured credentials.
  3. Create replication task with migration-type full-load-and-cdc.
  4. Run full load, enable CDC, and monitor replication lag.
  5. Validate data and perform cutover when caught up.
Key Takeaway

Full load plus CDC gives a tested target with minimal downtime at cutover; plan and test the timing carefully.

Concrete scenario

Imagine migrating an orders database with continuous activity. Perform the full load during a quiet window, enable CDC to stream new orders, and test the application against the target until it is fully synchronized.

Misconception

CDC replaces full load — false. CDC captures changes from a start position and does not provide historical rows prior to that position.

Pro tip

Enable validation early and monitor CDC lag; if lag rises, increase instance size or throttle write load during cutover tests.

screens.title: What is the Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)?
screens.narratorSegment: The Schema Conversion Tool is a companion to DMS for heterogeneous migrations. Its job is to analyze the source schema and custom code — stored procedures, functions, triggers, and views — and generate a compatible schema and code for the target engine when possible. SCT produces an assessment report that lists objects that were converted automatically and objects that require manual intervention. For example, when converting from Oracle to PostgreSQL, SCT will translate many data types and simple stored code constructs, but may flag proprietary PL/S Q L packages or vendor-specific functions for review. A valuable practical use of SCT is to run it early in the migration to estimate the manual effort needed and identify which application parts will require changes. A common mistake is deferring SCT until late in the process; by then conversion issues can cause project delays. After SCT generates the converted schema, apply it to the target database and then use DMS to migrate data into that converted structure. The key takeaway is that SCT reduces manual conversion work but does not eliminate it — plan for assessment, manual fixes, and thorough testing.

keyIdea.text: SCT converts schema and much custom code, and gives an assessment report flagging items needing manual conversion for heterogeneous migrations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Schema Conversion Tool
SCT overview

SCT analyzes source schema and custom code, converts compatible items to the target engine, and reports items needing manual conversion.

Assessment report

The report identifies converted objects and flags incompatible or proprietary code that requires manual rewriting before the target can support application logic.

Concrete example

When converting Oracle to PostgreSQL, SCT will translate many schema objects but will flag complex PL/SQL routines and vendor-specific functions for manual review and rewrite.

Key Takeaway

Run SCT early to estimate conversion effort, then plan manual work and testing before running DMS data migration.

screens.title: Designing a migration strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a migration strategy requires a sequence of decisions and verification steps. Start by assessing complexity: determine whether a migration is homogeneous or heterogeneous, measure database size, and identify stored code and features that may not convert cleanly. For heterogeneous scenarios run SCT to get an assessment report and estimate manual conversion effort. Next, size your replication instance to handle the full load and ongoing CDC throughput; under-sizing will introduce lag and extend cutover. Configure secure endpoints inside a VPC with appropriate security groups and encrypted connections to protect credentials and data in transit. In replication tasks, enable data validation so DMS can compare source and target rows and flag discrepancies. Plan your cutover with a clear checklist: finish schema conversion and apply the converted schema to the target, run a full load, start CDC, test application behavior against the target, then perform final validation and switch application connectivity. Common mistakes include not testing converted code, skipping validation, or ignoring endpoint security. The main insight is that careful assessment, sizing, security, and validation together produce predictable, low-risk cutovers. Designing a migration strategy means assess engine compatibility, run sct if needed, size replication instance, secure endpoints, enable validation, and plan a tested cutover.. In practical terms, assessment, sizing, security, validation, and cutover planning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Design strategy
Assess

Inventory engine type, code, and downtime needs.

Convert

Run SCT for heterogeneous migrations and apply converted schema to the target.

Migrate

Run DMS full load, enable CDC, and validate data before cutover.

Security and sizing

Place endpoints in a VPC, use security groups, encrypt in transit, and choose a replication instance class that matches migration throughput.

Validation and cutover

Enable DMS validation, run application tests against the target, and schedule a short cutover window for final synchronization and switching connections.

screens.title: Common migration mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes slow migrations and increase risk. The first is under-sizing the replication instance. When the instance lacks capacity, your full load takes longer and CDC lags behind the source, increasing the cutover window. Second, skipping schema conversion assessment or running SCT too late causes surprises when features or code don't behave on the target. Third, not enabling data validation leaves you blind to mismatches that can break application logic after cutover. Fourth, weak endpoint security or public accessibility exposes credentials and data in transit to risk. Finally, insufficient testing of the converted schema and application behavior on the target often leads to runtime failures. Avoid these errors by following a checklist: run SCT early for heterogeneous migrations, size your replication instance for measured throughput, secure endpoints inside a VPC with explicit security groups, enable DMS validation, and run end-to-end tests before cutover. A useful mindset is to treat migration as a repeatable process: document assumptions, run dry runs, capture metrics, and iterate until the validation results are consistently clean. That repeatability is what makes migrations predictable and safe for production systems.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Common Mistakes
Under-sizing replication instance

Insufficient CPU or network capacity increases migration time and CDC lag. Test with realistic load to size correctly.

Late SCT assessment

Running SCT late uncovers conversion work at the worst moment. Run SCT early to budget manual fixes.

Skipping validation

Without DMS validation you may end up with undetected row mismatches. Enable validation during test runs.

Weak security

Exposed endpoints or missing encryption put data at risk. Use VPC endpoints, security groups, and encrypted connections.

Pro tip

Run repeated dry runs and capture performance metrics to validate instance sizing and migration timing before production cutover.

screens.title: Conceptual walkthrough with CLI examples
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough summarizes the key CLI steps you'd perform when setting up a DMS migration. While we won't execute these commands here, understanding their role helps you organize resources and automation. First, you create a replication subnet group and a replication instance to run migrations. The create-replication-instance command provisions the managed compute that runs tasks. Next you create endpoints for source and target using create-endpoint; each endpoint includes engine name and connection information. Then you create a replication task that ties the instance and endpoints together, specifies table mappings, and chooses the migration type such as full-load-and-cdc. You might also set CDC start positions and enable data validation in the task settings. Finally, you start the replication task to run the migration. A common error is forgetting to replace ARN placeholders with actual values returned by create-endpoint and create-replication-instance; treat those ARNs as inputs to the replication-task creation. The practical point is to script these steps so they are repeatable, and to run them first in test environments. Below are the commands as a conceptual reference and not as executable copies in this environment.

keyIdea.text: Create replication instance and endpoints, then create and start replication tasks with full-load-and-cdc and validation enabled.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Conceptual CLI walkthrough
Prepare resources

Create a replication instance in a subnet group with appropriate security groups and no public access for production migrations.

Conceptual commands (reference)
aws dms create-replication-instance \
  --replication-instance-identifier my-dms-replication-instance \
  --replication-instance-class dms.t3.medium \
  --replication-subnet-group-identifier my-dms-subnet-group \
  --vpc-security-group-ids sg-xxxxxxxx \
  --publicly-accessible false

aws dms create-endpoint \
  --endpoint-identifier my-source-mysql \
  --endpoint-type source \
  --engine-name mysql \
  --mysql-settings '{ "ServerName": "your-ec2-mysql-ip", "Port": 3306, "Username": "your_mysql_user", "Password": "your_mysql_password", "DatabaseName": "your_source_db" }'

aws dms create-endpoint \
  --endpoint-identifier my-target-rds-mysql \
  --endpoint-type target \
  --engine-name mysql \
  --mysql-settings '{ "ServerName": "your-rds-endpoint", "Port": 3306, "Username": "your_rds_user", "Password": "your_rds_password", "DatabaseName": "your_target_db" }'

aws dms create-replication-task \
  --replication-task-identifier my-mysql-migration-task \
  --source-endpoint-arn arn:aws:dms:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:endpoint:SOURCE_ENDPOINT_ID \
  --target-endpoint-arn arn:aws:dms:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:endpoint:TARGET_ENDPOINT_ID \
  --replication-instance-arn arn:aws:dms:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:rep:REPLICATION_INSTANCE_ID \
  --migration-type full-load-and-cdc \
  --table-mappings '{"rules":[{"rule-type":"selection","rule-id":"1","object-locator":{"schema-name":"your_source_db","table-name":"%"},"filter-conditions":[]} ] }' \
  --cdc-start-position "now" \
  --data-validation-settings '{"EnableValidation":true}'

aws dms start-replication-task \
  --replication-task-arn arn:aws:dms:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:task:TASK_ID \
  --start-replication-task-type start-replication
Notes
  • Replace ARN placeholders with actual values returned by create commands.
  • Run these commands in a test environment before production.
Key Takeaway

Automate and script steps so migrations are repeatable and auditable across environments.

screens.title: A practical migration timeline
screens.narratorSegment: A clear timeline helps ensure migrations stay on schedule and within downtime targets. Start with assessment: inventory schema, measure data volume, and run SCT if needed. Next, prepare target infrastructure — create the target database and ensure network connectivity. Then, configure DMS resources: replication subnet group, replication instance, endpoints, and replication tasks. The migration phase begins with a full load during a controlled window, followed by enabling CDC to stream live changes. While CDC is running, perform functional and performance tests against the target to validate behavior. When testing shows the target is fully synchronized and application behavior is acceptable, schedule a short maintenance window for cutover: stop writes to the source, apply any final changes, run a last validation, and switch application connections to the target. After cutover, monitor application metrics and keep a fallback plan ready in case rollback is required. A common misconception is thinking cutover is a single click — it is a sequence of verification and switch steps. The core insight is to treat migration as a series of testable milestones so stakeholders can track progress and risks are visible at every step.

Milestones
  1. Assessment: Inventory schema and run SCT for heterogeneous migrations.

Real-world note

Each milestone produces artifacts: SCT reports, replication logs, validation reports, and application test results — collect them to reduce cutover risk.

fullNarratorScript:
Migrating a running database to AWS is one of the most concrete problems a solutions architect will solve. In this lesson you'll see the complementary roles of AWS Database Migration Service and the Schema Conversion Tool. DMS is designed to move and synchronize data reliably across engines and platforms, while SCT focuses on converting schema elements and custom database code when engines differ. Together they reduce downtime by letting you perform a full initial copy and then continuously replicate changes until cutover. We'll highlight common migration types, the core components you must configure, and the practical trade-offs you will face, such as replication instance sizing, endpoint security, and validation. You will also be shown a short conceptual walkthrough that mirrors a real migration: prepare source and target, run schema conversion for heterogeneous moves, then use DMS to perform a full load followed by change data capture to keep systems in sync. By the end of this module you'll understand when to use SCT, how DMS handles continuous replication, and what testing and validation steps prevent common failures during cutover. Consider one immediate question as you begin: what level of downtime can your application tolerate?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify migration challenges, explain DMS capabilities, use SCT for heterogeneous conversions, and design a migration strategy that balances downtime and risk. First, you'll learn to identify common challenges like data integrity, compatibility between engines, and limiting downtime. Recognizing these problems helps you pick the right migration type and tools. Second, you'll learn how DMS supports both homogeneous and heterogeneous migrations, how it moves data, and how continuous replication keeps target systems synchronized. Third, you'll practice using the Schema Conversion Tool to assess and convert schema and custom code when engines differ. This helps you estimate manual work and prioritize tests. Fourth, you'll design a migration approach that combines a full initial load, Change Data Capture for ongoing changes, and data validation to confirm correctness. Each objective focuses on real decisions you must make: what to convert automatically, how to size a replication instance, and how to secure endpoints. These skills let you plan migrations that meet business downtime constraints while protecting application behavior and data integrity.

Let's take those objectives a layer deeper and relate them to concrete tasks you'll perform. When you identify migration challenges you will inventory schema, stored code, and data volume, and then define acceptable downtime. That inventory informs whether you need SCT for code conversion. When you explain DMS capabilities you will choose between homogeneous moves where only data transfer is required, and heterogeneous moves where schema conversion is essential. Practically, that means using DMS replication instances to carry data, and configuring endpoints and tasks with appropriate table mappings. When using SCT, you'll run an assessment report that highlights items requiring manual conversion; you will use that report to estimate engineering effort and prioritize tests. Finally, when designing a migration strategy you'll size the replication instance, enable encryption and VPC connectivity for endpoints, and enable DMS validation to compare source and target rows. Each objective ties to a verification step: run test migrations, exercise the application against the target, and perform a final validation before cutover. These steps reduce surprises and protect production traffic during migration.

Migrating a production database is not just a data copy exercise — it's an exercise in preserving application behavior, integrity, and availability. The core challenges are maintaining data integrity across millions of rows, minimizing downtime so user-facing systems remain responsive, and handling compatibility issues between database engines if you change platforms. For many organizations the highest priority is limiting the cutover window so the business isn't disrupted. That requirement drives the use of an initial full load followed by continuous replication. A concrete example is a web application backed by an on-premises Oracle database that must move to PostgreSQL on RDS. You cannot simply copy data; stored procedures and proprietary S Q L might behave differently on the target. This is where assessments and tools become critical: the Schema Conversion Tool analyzes schema and code, identifying items that can be converted automatically and those that will need manual work. A common misconception is thinking that data movement alone solves migration — in heterogeneous scenarios, schema and code conversion are equally important. The takeaway is to treat migration as a systems project: inventory, plan for compatibility, and design for validation and rollback before you run the first replication task.

AWS Database Migration Service is a managed service that performs the heavy lifting of moving data between sources and targets. At heart, DMS orchestrates a replication instance that connects to a source endpoint and a target endpoint, reads data from the source, and applies it to the target. It supports relational databases, data warehouses, NoSQL stores, and other data stores. A homogeneous migration is straightforward because the engines match — DMS focuses on data transfer, optionally with minor schema adjustments. For heterogeneous migrations DMS still moves the data, but schema and code conversion are handled by the Schema Conversion Tool. A practical sketch of the DMS architecture helps: replication instances are managed compute resources that run migration tasks, endpoints store connection details and credentials, and replication tasks define which tables to migrate and whether to capture ongoing changes. A common pitfall is under-sizing the replication instance. If the instance can't keep up, the migration is slow and CDC lag grows. The important takeaway is to treat DMS as an orchestration platform — configure instance size, secure endpoints inside your VPC, and enable validation to ensure the target matches the source.

Understanding whether you're performing a homogeneous or heterogeneous migration is one of the first architectural decisions you must make. A homogeneous migration occurs when source and target engines are the same, for example MySQL to MySQL. In that case, your primary work is transferring data; DMS handles the copy, continuous replication, and validation with minimal schema conversion. A heterogeneous migration happens when database engines differ, such as Oracle to PostgreSQL or S Q L Server to MySQL. Heterogeneous moves are more complex because schema structures, data types, and procedural code differ. DMS remains responsible for data movement, but schema and code conversion requires the Schema Conversion Tool. SCT analyzes the source schema and custom database code, automatically converts compatible elements, and produces an assessment report that flags items needing manual attention. A concrete example: migrating Oracle PL/S Q L packages to PostgreSQL functions may require manual rewriting for complex logic; SCT will identify those functions and estimate conversion work. A common misconception is believing DMS will convert all stored code automatically — it will not. The practical consequence is to run SCT early, estimate manual effort, and reserve time for testing and application adjustments before cutover.

A reliable migration requires understanding the three pillars of DMS: replication instance, endpoints, and replication tasks. The replication instance is managed compute that reads from the source and writes to the target. You choose an instance class based on throughput and latency requirements; under-sizing commonly causes replication lag. Endpoints capture connection details for source and target databases — host, port, credentials, and engine type — and they should be secured inside your VPC with proper security groups. Replication tasks bind these together and define what to move and how: table mappings, filters, transformation rules, and the migration type. DMS supports full load, change data capture, or full-load plus CDC. For a typical low-downtime strategy you run a full load to copy existing rows, then enable CDC to apply ongoing changes until the target is caught up. A practical check: enable data validation in the replication task to compare rows and catch drift. A misconception to avoid is treating replication tasks as a one-time setting; refine mappings and validation rules during testing to ensure the target schema receives data in the expected shape. The core insight is that correct configuration across these components prevents surprises during cutover.

A low-downtime migration commonly uses a two-phase approach: an initial full load followed by Change Data Capture. The full load copies existing rows from source to target; CDC then streams new and changed transactions to the target so it stays synchronized. In practice you start by creating endpoints, sizing your replication instance, and running a replication task in full-load-and-cdc mode. The full load runs first and populates the target. CDC continues to capture inserts, updates, and deletes on the source until you are ready to cut over. This approach lets you test the application on the target while production continues to write to the source. A concrete example: copy a million-row orders table during off-peak hours, then enable CDC to apply ongoing orders as they arrive. Once the target is fully caught up, perform a short maintenance window for final validation and switch application connectivity. A common misconception is relying on CDC alone to reconstruct historical state; CDC only captures changes from a start position and does not replace a full initial load for historical data. The key insight is to coordinate full load, CDC, and validation to achieve a predictable cutover with minimal downtime.

The Schema Conversion Tool is a companion to DMS for heterogeneous migrations. Its job is to analyze the source schema and custom code — stored procedures, functions, triggers, and views — and generate a compatible schema and code for the target engine when possible. SCT produces an assessment report that lists objects that were converted automatically and objects that require manual intervention. For example, when converting from Oracle to PostgreSQL, SCT will translate many data types and simple stored code constructs, but may flag proprietary PL/S Q L packages or vendor-specific functions for review. A valuable practical use of SCT is to run it early in the migration to estimate the manual effort needed and identify which application parts will require changes. A common mistake is deferring SCT until late in the process; by then conversion issues can cause project delays. After SCT generates the converted schema, apply it to the target database and then use DMS to migrate data into that converted structure. The key takeaway is that SCT reduces manual conversion work but does not eliminate it — plan for assessment, manual fixes, and thorough testing.

Designing a migration strategy requires a sequence of decisions and verification steps. Start by assessing complexity: determine whether a migration is homogeneous or heterogeneous, measure database size, and identify stored code and features that may not convert cleanly. For heterogeneous scenarios run SCT to get an assessment report and estimate manual conversion effort. Next, size your replication instance to handle the full load and ongoing CDC throughput; under-sizing will introduce lag and extend cutover. Configure secure endpoints inside a VPC with appropriate security groups and encrypted connections to protect credentials and data in transit. In replication tasks, enable data validation so DMS can compare source and target rows and flag discrepancies. Plan your cutover with a clear checklist: finish schema conversion and apply the converted schema to the target, run a full load, start CDC, test application behavior against the target, then perform final validation and switch application connectivity. Common mistakes include not testing converted code, skipping validation, or ignoring endpoint security. The main insight is that careful assessment, sizing, security, and validation together produce predictable, low-risk cutovers. Designing a migration strategy means assess engine compatibility, run sct if needed, size replication instance, secure endpoints, enable validation, and plan a tested cutover.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
